title: Chapter 54: The Night of Masks, Part 5 of 5: The Duke's Glass
html:
The Duke found her there, still looking at the floor round the brass box, a little before the eleventh bell. He did not say anything at first. He stood beside her with his glass of Marrowmere, and looked at the floor too.
Then he said, very quietly, "I have it, you know."
Lyra did not look up.
"Your memory," said the Duke. "The one you gave me. A week ago, in my gallery, in the dark. The price." He turned the glass a little in his ringed fingers, and the pale gold wine caught the light. "It's on the shelf. In a jar. With a lens in front of it, like all the others. Mr. Pennick labeled it for me. T. Front hall. Given."
She remembered the gallery. The black room, with its two hundred glowing jars, and the lenses, and the old man with the gray to his shoulders. And the moment when it left her. The feeling of a door closing very gently in a house far away. And three words, going away with it, very faint, in her mother's voice. Keep them safe.
She had four memories of her mother now. She counted them at night like coins. The brushing. The rain on Crown Walk. The empty chair. The song. There had been five.
"I've never opened one," said the Duke. "Not in forty years. Not one. You know that. I told you." He paused. "I looked at yours. Through the lens. Once. On Saturday night, after you'd gone. I sat in front of it for an hour."
Lyra looked at him then.
"I'm sorry," said the Duke. "I should not have. It wasn't mine to look at. But I had loved her very much, you see, your mother. In my way. In the way a fat lonely man loves a woman who is kind to him at parties." He did not look at Lyra. He looked at the brass box. "And I wanted to see her once more. That's all."
"What did you see?"
She heard her own voice. It came out of the still white mask very small.
The Duke was quiet for a moment.
"The hall on Crown Walk," he said. "At night. The lamps on the landings. The black and white floor. And a little girl in a white nightgown on the bottom stair, the wide one. With her feet bare. Very cross, because she had been woken up." A small sound in his throat that might have been a laugh. "You were very cross. You had a face like a thundercloud. Nine years old."
Lyra stood very still.
"And your mother came across the hall," said the Duke. "In her traveling cloak. The dark blue one, with the fur in the hood. And her gray gloves. And knelt down on the black and white floor in front of you, on the marble, in her cloak. And took your face in her hands. Like this." He did not do it. He held his great soft ringed hands up a little, in the air, as if there were a face between them. "And held it. And looked at you for a long time. And you stopped being cross. You looked back at her. You didn't know what was happening. But you knew something was."
The quartet behind the palms was playing something slow.
"And she said," said the Duke. "She said, Lyra. Keep them safe. Count them. Every day. Keep them safe until I come."
The dam held. Lyra did not know how.
"Until I come," she said.
"Until I come," said the Duke. "That's what she said. I heard it through the lens. Quite clearly." He lowered his hands. "And then she kissed your forehead, and stood up, and went out of the front door. And Oren was holding it. And Tibbs was on the box. And the door shut. And you sat on the bottom step in your nightgown and counted the stairs. Out loud. Up to the first landing. Fourteen. Over and over." He was quiet. "That's where the memory ends. On fourteen."
Lyra looked down at her gloved hands.
"Them," she said.
"Yes," said the Duke. "I wondered about that. All Saturday night. I sat in front of the jar and wondered. Keep them safe. I thought she meant you and your brother. And your father, perhaps." He turned the glass. "But she didn't say your brother. She didn't say Rowan. She didn't say your father. She said them. And she said count them." He looked at Lyra. "You don't count two, my dear. Two isn't counting. You count when there are more."
Nobody said anything for a while.
The chandelier swung slowly on its chain. The vials glowed on their velvet. Somewhere across the room, Lady Ashcombe's little white dog barked, once, and was shushed.
"I'll give it back to you," said the Duke. "If you want it. After. If there's an after. I'll take it off the shelf myself and put it in your hands." He paused. "I don't know if it can go back. Pennick says sometimes it can, if it's done very gently, by somebody who knows the old ways. Sometimes it can't. But you can have the jar. And look at it through the lens, the way I did. And see her."
Lyra did not answer at once.
Then she said, "Keep it."
The Duke looked at her.
"Keep it for me," said Lyra. "On your shelf. With the lens. Where it's safe." She looked at the brass box. "I don't need it tonight. I know what it says now. You've told me." She swallowed. "Keep them safe. Count them. Until I come. That's enough. That's all I need from it. The rest is just a little girl on a stair being cross."
"She was very charming," said the Duke. "The little girl. Even cross."
"I don't remember her," said Lyra.
"No," said the Duke of Marrow gently. "No. But I do. Now. And so does the jar. That's what the gallery is for, my dear. That's all it was ever for. Two hundred and eleven things that somebody couldn't bear to lose, and couldn't bear to keep. And an old fool who sits with them in the dark." He lifted his glass of Marrowmere, and looked at it, and did not drink it. "I'll keep her for you. As long as you like."
Across the river, through the glass of the dome and the falling snow, the great bell of the Ministry began to ring the eleventh hour.
And in her box opposite the bronze doors, Lady Vivienne lifted a little silver bell.
The Bidding
At the eleventh bell Lady Vivienne rang a little silver bell from her box, and the bidding began.
It was not like an auction. Lyra had been to an auction. She had stood at the back of the hall on Crown Walk two years ago, at eighteen, in a borrowed cloak with the hood up, and watched a man with a hammer sell her mother's harp, and her father's books, and the chandelier from the hall, one by one, to men who shouted numbers. It had been loud and quick and ugly.
This was quiet.
Nobody shouted. Nobody raised a hand. Servants in plum went round the room with silver trays, and on each tray there was a pile of white cards, small and stiff, the size of a playing card, with a plum border, and a little silver pencil on a chain. And people took a card, and turned their backs, and wrote on it. Very small. Shielding it with their hands, the way children shield their slates at school. A lot number. A sum. A name. And then they folded the card in half, and walked, quite slowly, without hurrying, as if they were only strolling, to the middle of the room. To the brass box. And dropped the card in through the long narrow slot in the top.
It made a small sound. A soft dry whisper, going down inside the brass. Like a leaf falling into a well.
And the woman in the dark green coat at the little table beside the box looked up at each one, and wrote in her ledger. Not the sum. She could not see the sum. Just a mark. One mark for each card. Lyra watched her pen move. One. And then again. Two. Counting.
The man in the black half-mask in the plain chair on the other side of the box did not look up at all. He sat with his hand on the wooden case and watched the room.
They went up to the box one at a time, all through the eleventh hour. Lords and ladies and councillors and their wives. Lyra watched them. She could not stop watching them. Lady Harriet Langley in her blue feathers, going up with a card held against her chest and her face pink under the mask, for Lot 17. The boy at the fair. Lyra was sure of it. One of the Fennimore boys, very red now, very unsteady, dropping his card and having to pick it up off the floor by the box while everybody pretended not to see. Lord Ost. Lady Ost, separately, a little after, not looking at her husband. The Warden of Saint Clement's, in his black, very slowly, with his card held out in front of him as if it might bite.
The Duke went up once.
He took a card off a tray and wrote on it with the little silver pencil, quite openly, without shielding it, and Lyra saw what he wrote. Lot 12. Courage, common. Sixty-one crowns. Marrow. And he folded it and walked up to the box with his great soft rolling walk and dropped it in. And came back.
"For a nervous child," he said, when he saw her looking. "It says so on the card. I've a house full of them, I'm told. On Crown Walk."
She did not say anything. She could not.
"Oh, I shan't give it to any of them," said the Duke. "Silas said nothing sweet for a year. I should think courage counts as sweet." He looked at his untouched glass of Marrowmere. "I just didn't want anybody else to have it."
The Treasurer went up. Lyra watched him go. Tall and lean in his gray silk with the silver in it, with his plain silver mask on now, walking quite slowly across the black and white floor, nodding to people as he passed. He had a card in his hand. He did not write on it at the box. He had written it somewhere else, before. He dropped it into the slot, and the dry whisper went down into the brass, and he stood for a moment by the box, beside the woman in the dark green coat, and said something to her. Lyra could not hear what. The woman did not look up. She wrote a mark in her ledger.
And then the Treasurer turned his head, and looked at the man in the plain chair.
Just for a moment. Through the plain silver mask.
The man in the black half-mask did not look back.
The Treasurer bowed. A small bow, from the neck. And touched his gold watch chain, once, with one finger. And walked away.
The Inquisitor did not go up. He was in the gallery again, in his box, beside the girl in white. He did not take a card. He sat with one arm along the rail and watched.
And near the half hour, Lucian went up.
He came from beside the plain chair. Lyra did not see the man in the black mask give him anything. But Lucian had a card in his hand. One of the white cards with the plum border, folded. He walked the five steps from the chair to the box, counting them, Lyra saw his lips move, and dropped the card through the slot. And walked the five steps back. And stood beside the chair again, with his black book held against his chest.
The woman in the dark green coat made a mark in her ledger.
The room had seen. Lyra felt it see. A little ripple went round it, under the music, under the voices. A little catch of breath. And then nothing. Nobody said anything. Nobody looked. Everybody knew.
Three men asked me for it this winter, her aunt had said, on Friday, in the white room. One tapped. One looked at his watch, and didn't. And one sent his card.
Lyra looked across the room at her aunt.
Cressida was standing by her table near the bronze doors, alone, in white silk, very still, with her untouched glass in her hand. She was looking at the brass box. Her white beautiful face was perfectly calm.
The glass in her hand was shaking.
Lyra looked away.
She looked for the gold coat.
She had been looking for it all night, without seeming to. Following it round the room out of the corner of her eye, the way you follow a candle in a dark house. A tall sour man in Marrow gold with a stiff left leg and a decanter of pale wine on a tray, limping from table to table, pouring for the Duke when the Duke held out his glass, and standing by the wall when he did not, with his white-gloved hands folded and his long sour face showing nothing at all. Nobody had looked at him. Not once. Not the Weigher. Not the Lady's servants in plum, who went past him a hundred times. Not the Inquisitor, in the gallery, who looked at everybody. He was part of the furniture, the Duke had said. Like the brass box.
At the half hour after the eleventh bell, he was by the wall near the gallery stair, with his tray.
At twenty to midnight he was not.
Lyra did not see him go. She looked at the place by the wall where he had been, and there was a tray there, on a little gilt table, with the cut-glass decanter on it, and two glasses, and nobody. And she looked along the wall, toward the back of the room, behind the gallery stair, where a low door led through to the passages behind the hall, and the kitchens, and the kitchen yard. The servants' way. A door with plum velvet over it that the Lady's people went in and out of all night with trays. It was swinging, very slightly, on its hinges. As if somebody had just gone through it.
She did not look at it long.
She looked at the Duke instead. He was talking to Lady Ashcombe about her dog. He did not look at the door either. But his big soft hand, holding his glass of Marrowmere, had gone very still.
And from somewhere far away, very faint, high up, so faint that she could not be sure she had heard it at all, through the glass of the dome and the falling snow and the music of the quartet behind the palms, there came a sound.
A whistle.
One long one.
Thin and high and steady. Going on, and on. And stopping.
One long, everything's all right.
Nobody else heard it. Lyra was sure nobody else heard it. The music went on. The voices went on. The man in the black half-mask sat in his plain chair with his hand on his wooden case. The woman in the dark green coat wrote in her ledger.
But in the gallery, in the box three along from the Lady's, the girl in the long white coat with the twelve silver buttons had turned her head.
Not toward the room. Up. Toward the dome. Toward the far side of it, where the glass met the black stone of the roof. And the great lead gutter. And something lying very flat in it, against the glass.
She looked at it for a long moment.
Then she turned her head back. And looked down at the room. And folded her white-gloved hands on the rail. And did not say anything to the slight gray man beside her, who was watching the brass box, and humming.
A Quarter to Midnight
At a quarter before midnight the Lady came down from her gallery, and the room went to the brass box like water going down a drain.
Nobody told it to. Nobody rang a bell. Lady Vivienne simply stood up out of her chair in her box opposite the bronze doors, in her violet, with her necklace of little lights at her throat, and came out of the box, and along the gallery, and down the gallery stair behind the iron pillar, slowly, one step at a time, with her black lace fan closed in her hand and Remy behind her. No. Not Remy. Lyra looked again. A servant in plum, carrying her train. Remy was not there. Remy had not been in the box since the eleventh bell.
And as she came down, the room turned. And moved. All of it. Five hundred people in masks, leaving the glass tables with their glowing vials, putting down their glasses, drifting, not hurrying, toward the middle of the room. Toward the brass box. Toward the little clear space round it on the black and white floor. And stopping at the edge of the ring of black squares, all round, in a great circle, three and four deep, the way people stop at the edge of a pond.
Lyra went with them. She could not have done anything else. The Duke's arm under her hand went, and she went with it.
She found herself at the front. At the very edge of the ring. Close enough to the black squares that the toe of her mother's gray kid slipper was touching the line where the white square ended and the black began. She did not know how she had got there. The Duke had brought her. She looked up at him. He was looking at the box.
Across the ring, on the other side, the plain chair. And the man in the black half-mask sitting in it, with his hand on the wooden case on Lucian's arm. He had not moved.
And beside the chair, standing, a slight gray man in a plain white mask, with his hands behind his back.
The Inquisitor had come down. He was standing right beside the brass box, at the edge of the black ring, the way he had said he would. Close to the man in the chair. Not looking at him. Looking at the floor.
And beside the Inquisitor, a little behind him, a girl in a long white coat with twelve silver buttons. Very straight. With her hands at her sides.
On the other side of the box, at her little table, the woman in the dark green coat had closed her ledger. She was standing now. With her white-gloved hands flat on the closed book.
And near the bronze doors, at the back of the crowd, a little apart, alone, a woman in white silk with three ropes of pearls and five silver pins in her hair. Not coming forward. Watching.
And somewhere in the crowd, tall and lean in gray silk, with a plain silver mask, a man with a gold watch chain across his waistcoat. Lyra could not see him. She knew he was there.
Lady Vivienne came across the floor.
The crowd opened for her. She came through it in her violet, with her train held up behind her by the servant in plum, and her long pale face without a mask, and the little colored lights at her throat, and stopped at the edge of the black ring. Opposite the plain chair. Opposite the man in the black half-mask.
She looked at him across the box.
She did not bow. Lyra saw that. She was the only person in the room who had not bowed when he came in, except the woman at the Fourth Desk, and she did not bow now. She stood very straight, with her fan closed in her hand, and looked at him. And he looked at her. Through the black mask. For a long moment. Neither of them said anything.
Then Lady Vivienne turned to the room.
"The Fourth Tier," she said.
And lifted her closed fan, and struck the side of the brass box with it. Once.
It rang. A deep soft brassy note, like a great gong, very low, going down into the floor. Lyra felt it in her feet. She felt it in her teeth.
And under her feet, under the black and white marble, very deep, something answered.
A groan.
Long and low and heavy. Like a ship's timbers in a storm. Like a great beast waking up underground and turning over. It came up through the floor into her slippers, into her legs, into her spine. The crowd round the ring went very still. Some of them took a step back. Lyra did not. She could not. Her feet would not move.
The groan went on. And with it, now, a sound under the groan. A slow deep clanking. Iron on iron. Regular. Clank. A pause. Clank. Like a great chain being wound onto a great drum, one link at a time, by somebody turning a handle very slowly. Two somebodies. Very big. Very patient. Who did not see anything, and did not stop anything, and only turned the handle.
Big Gideon and Saul. Right there by the way out. Turning the handle.
And the floor began to move.
The ring of black squares round the brass box. All of it. All at once. The whole wide black ring, from the foot of the box to the toe of Lyra's slipper, began to sink. Slowly. Very slowly. Going down. The white squares outside it stayed where they were. The brass box in the middle stayed where it was, on a pillar of black iron that she could see now, as the floor went down round it, going down and down into the dark. But the black ring sank away from under the box and from under the edges of the crowd, smoothly, evenly, like a great round lid being lowered into a well.
An inch. Two. A hand's width.
The cold came up.
It came up out of the widening crack between the white floor and the sinking black ring all round the box, all at once, in a long breath. Cold. Colder than the street. Colder than the garden door. The cold of a cellar, of a place under the ground where ice is kept, and the smell with it. Wet stone. Iron. And something else. Something Lyra had smelled once before, in a white room on Crown Walk, in a white chair, with a silver cup in front of her that she had not drunk from. Something like the inside of a jar that has been sealed for a very long time.
The crowd breathed in, all together, and stepped back.
Lyra did not step back.
She stood at the very edge, with the toe of her slipper on the white marble and the black ring going down and down in front of her, a foot now, two feet, and looked down into the gap. Into the dark. It was very dark down there. She could see the black ring going down, and the iron pillar under the brass box, and the edge of the floor she was standing on, which was thick, a foot thick, solid marble, and under it nothing. Just the dark. And the cold coming up out of it. And the slow deep clank of the chain, coming up from somewhere far below.
And she thought: He's down there.
Somewhere in that dark. Under her feet. With his stiff leg and his borrowed face and his white cotton gloves over his gray hands. On a stair, or in a passage of glass that knew him, or in a cold room full of sealed things, with Remy beside him and the Lady's key in his blood. Looking for a black wooden case with a silver clasp, and a folded square on it, and her father's last evening inside.
Lot 41 goes up last.
She counted.
She could not help it. She had always counted. She counted now, standing at the edge of the hole in the floor of the Memory Bourse, with five hundred masks at her back and the cold coming up into her face and the clank of the chain coming up under her feet.
One.
The black ring went down another hand's width.
Two.
Across the hole, on the far side, by the plain chair, the Inquisitor had stepped to the very edge, as she had. He was looking down into the dark too. With his hands behind his back. With his head a little on one side.
Three.
And then he lifted his head. And looked across the hole. Across the brass box on its iron pillar, and the sinking black ring, and the cold dark gap between them.
At her.
Through his plain white mask. With his pale tired eyes. The way he had looked up at the tower window from the step of Saint Bride's.
And he smiled.
Not much. Just the corners of the mouth, under the edge of the mask. The smile of a man who has set a table very carefully, and seen his guests sit down, and is waiting for the first course.
Four.
And from somewhere far below, from the dark under the floor, from under the cold and the clank of the chain, very faint, so faint that she could not be sure she had heard it at all, there came a sound that was not iron, and not stone, and not the groan of the floor.
A voice.
A boy's voice. Humming.
Three notes. And then the rest. Going up, and up, and hanging.
Not her mother's song. A different tune. Lower. Slower. A carrying tune. The kind men hum when they are carrying something heavy a long way.
Gideon's father's tune.
Lyra stood at the edge of the hole with her hands pressed together in Madame Hesper's gloves, under the falling-gold sky of the dome, and did not breathe.
Five, she counted.
And the floor went on going down.
